name: Dropped third strike, bases loaded, 2 outs
offense: The batter can run because there are two outs, even though first base is occupied. Everyone runs: every runner is forced to move up. Batter: drop the bat and sprint to first right away.
defense: Every base is a force. The simplest out is often for the catcher to pick up the ball and step on home plate, or throw to first. Don't rush into a wild throw: one clean force ends the inning.
common_mistakes: Batter walks back to the dugout thinking it's over; runners stop; catcher tags the batter late or throws wildly instead of taking the sure force at home.
verify_note: Reviewed by our umpire on 2026-10-25. Strategy in our words; general baseball/softball rule logic. Applies only where the uncaught-third-strike rule is in effect. Coach/umpire to confirm.

name: Dropped third strike, runner on first, 1 out
offense: With first base occupied and fewer than two outs, the batter is out and can't run, whether or not the catcher holds the pitch. The runner on first is NOT forced; he may try to advance at his own risk.
defense: The batter is already out. Don't throw to first; watch the runner. Keep the ball in front, call 'batter's out' loudly so the infield knows, and only throw if the runner is trying to advance.
common_mistakes: Defense throws to first for a batter who is already out and lets the runner take extra bases; batter runs when he can't and draws a throw that helps no one.
verify_note: Reviewed by our umpire on 2026-10-25. Strategy in our words; general baseball/softball rule logic. Applies only where the uncaught-third-strike rule is in effect. Coach/umpire to confirm.

name: Dropped third strike, runner on third, 1 out
offense: First base is open, so the batter can run: sprint to first the moment the ball gets away. The runner on third watches the catcher: if the catcher throws to first, that's often the chance to break for home.
defense: Tag the batter if he's close, or throw to first. Before throwing, check the runner on third; the corner infielders should call it out. A rushed throw can give away the winning run.
common_mistakes: Batter doesn't run because he thinks strike three ends it; runner on third doesn't read the throw; catcher throws to first without looking the runner back.

name: Runner hit by a fair batted ball, bases loaded, no outs
offense: One out, and the inning isn't over. A runner hit by a fair batted ball that no fielder has touched is out, and the ball is dead at that moment, even if it later rolls foul. Nothing after the dead ball counts. The batter is awarded first base and only forced runners move up one base, so with the bases loaded: the batter goes to first, the runner from first to second, the runner from second to third, and no run scores. Coaches: when you hear 'dead ball', stop calling for runners to go and let the umpires place them.
defense: Once the umpire calls dead ball, tags and throws don't count, however good they were: hold the ball and let the umpires place the runners. The key judgment is whether a fielder touched the ball before it hit the runner. If she did, the ball stays live and the runner isn't out unless she interfered on purpose, so the tags that followed would count.
common_mistakes: The umpire calls the runner out but doesn't kill the play loudly, so everyone keeps playing; a second umpire calls more outs on a ball that was already dead; coaches yell players into extra running and tagging; the crew changes a call because of the noise instead of getting together. Fix: 'Time! Dead ball!' with both arms up, a quick crew conference, then one calm explanation to each coach.
verify_note: Reviewed by our umpire on 2026-10-25. Our wording of general softball rule logic: an untouched fair batted ball hitting a runner before it passes an infielder makes the runner out and the ball dead; the batter gets first and only forced runners advance. name: Slow roller rolls foul, then back fair before first base
offense: It's a fair ball, so the batter is a runner and the out at first stands. A ground ball that hasn't reached first or third base isn't foul just because it crossed the line: it's judged where it stops or where a fielder first touches it. This one rolled foul, came back, and was picked up in fair territory, so it was fair and in play. Umpires usually signal a fair ball by pointing toward fair territory without saying anything; only foul is called out loud. Batter: run on every ball you hit until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!'
defense: Pick the ball up and make the play: step on first or throw there. A slow roller near the line that's still rolling can be left alone; if it stops or you touch it in foul territory before it reaches the base, it's foul. Fielders, like batters, play until the umpire stops it.
common_mistakes: The batter stands at the plate because the ball crossed the line once; the fielder picks it up and freezes; the umpire's fair signal is late or small, so nobody sees it; coaches on both sides shout directions and the players try to learn the rule in the middle of the play. Fix: the plate umpire points fair clearly the moment the ball is touched in fair territory, and coaches teach 'run until you hear foul' at practice, not during the play.
verify_note: Reviewed by our umpire on 2026-10-25. Our wording of the general fair/foul rule for a ground ball before first or third base (baseball and softball). No rulebook definition text is loaded yet (see gaps.csv). Fair or foul is the umpire's judgment and can't be protested (F015, F087, F199, F032). Scenario from Sean (2026-10-23).

name: Fly ball with a runner on first, fewer than 2 outs
offense: Take a few steps off the base and read the ball. With fewer than two outs, if it's caught you must get back and touch first before you can go anywhere, and the defense can throw behind you for a double play. If it drops, run hard: you're forced to second the moment it lands. On a very deep fly, you can tag up and try for second after the catch, but only if the throw can't beat you.
defense: Catch it, then look at the runner. If they're off the base, throw behind them to first for the double play. If they tagged and broke for second, hit the cutoff.
common_mistakes: The runner sprints on contact and gets doubled off; the runner stays glued to first on a ball that drops and is forced out at second; the runner forgets to go back and touch first before trying to advance.
verify_note: Drafted by Claude on 2026-10-25 from Sean's list of common base-running mistakes. Strategy from the practice sheet; tag-up rule in our own words. No rulebook text for retouching after a catch is loaded yet (see gaps.csv). Umpire to review, then set verified.

name: Fly ball with a runner on third, fewer than 2 outs
offense: Go back to third and tag up. Leave as soon as the fielder first touches the ball and sprint home. On a short fly or an infield pop-up, stay on the base unless your coach sends you. If you leave before the fielder touches the ball, the defense can appeal and you're out.
defense: Catch it and throw home through the cutoff. If the runner left early, tag third base or the runner and appeal to the umpire. Some leagues allow only live-ball appeals, so make the appeal before the next pitch.
common_mistakes: The runner goes halfway from third on a deep fly and can't score after the catch; the runner leaves before the catch; the runner jogs home and is thrown out.

name: Ground ball with a runner on first
offense: Run hard to second on contact. When the batter hits a fair ground ball, the batter needs first base, so you're forced to leave it. There's no waiting to see if it gets through, and there's no going back.
defense: Take the sure out. Older teams turn two, second base then first. Younger teams get the force at second or the out at first. Once the batter is out at first, the runner isn't forced any more, so a tag is needed to get them.
common_mistakes: The runner waits to see if the ball gets through and is forced out easily; the runner goes back to first and ends up on the same base as the batter; the runner stops halfway thinking the ball was caught.

name: Ground ball with the bases loaded, fewer than 2 outs
offense: Everyone runs. With the bases full, every runner is forced as soon as the batter hits a fair ground ball. Runner on third: sprint home, wherever the ball is hit. Nobody stops to look and nobody goes back.
defense: The force is on at every base, so step on the base instead of chasing a tag. The easiest out is often at home or at first. Older teams can turn home to first.
common_mistakes: The runner on third holds because the ball was hit to the left side; runners stop and watch; the catcher tries to tag the runner instead of stepping on home plate.

name: Ground ball with a runner on second, first base open
offense: You're not forced, so read where the ball goes. If it's hit in front of you (to the shortstop or third baseman), stay unless it gets through. If it's hit behind you (to the right side), run hard to third. With two outs, run on contact.
defense: Look the runner back to second before throwing to first. If the runner breaks on a ball to the left side, throw to third for the tag.
common_mistakes: The runner runs into a tag on a ball hit right to the shortstop; the runner holds on a ball to the right side and gives up an easy base.

name: Two outs, ball in play with runners on
offense: Run on contact, on everything: ground balls, line drives and fly balls. A catch ends the inning anyway, so there's nothing to tag up for. A runner on second should run hard and expect to score on a hit.
defense: Get the easiest out: a force at the nearest base or the out at first.
common_mistakes: Runners go halfway or tag up out of habit; runners stop to watch a fly ball; nobody reminds the runners that there are two outs.

name: Two runners end up on the same base
offense: Stay on the base and look at your coach; don't walk off. The base belongs to the runner who was there first, unless that runner was forced to leave it, in which case it belongs to the runner behind. The runner who doesn't own the base can be tagged out even while standing on it. If you're the lead runner and the base behind you is open, your coach may send you back there.
defense: Tag both runners, then let the umpire rule. Only the runner who isn't entitled to the base is out.
common_mistakes: Both runners step off thinking one is already out, and both are tagged; the fielder tags only one runner; coaches argue instead of asking the umpire which runner owns the base.

name: Batter runs through first base
offense: Run through first base at full speed. Touch the front edge of the bag, keep running a few steps past it, then slow down and look to your right, toward foul territory, to find the ball. Come back to first right away. You're allowed to run past first and come back without being tagged out, as long as you don't try to go to second.
defense: Stretch toward the throw with your foot on the base, then get out of the runner's path after the catch.
common_mistakes: The runner slows down to stop on the bag and is out by a step; the runner dives or slides into first, which is slower; the runner jogs on a routine ground ball and can't take advantage of a wild throw.

name: Batter overruns first and turns toward second (umpire's judgment)
offense: After you run through first, come straight back and don't make any move toward second unless you're really going. If the umpire judges that you tried to go to second, you lose the protection for overrunning the base and can be tagged out before you get back. Which way you turn doesn't decide it by itself: the umpire judges whether you made an attempt to advance.
defense: If the runner makes a move toward second, tag them, then let the umpire make the call.
common_mistakes: The runner drifts toward second while looking for the ball and is tagged; fans and coaches shout that the runner turned the wrong way, as if the direction alone decides it; players and coaches argue the call. Whether the runner tried to advance is the umpire's judgment, so the call stands.

name: Fly ball that clearly won't be caught, runner on first
offense: If the ball is clearly going to drop (over the outfielder's head, into a gap, or far from every fielder), run right away. The moment it lands you're forced to second, so freezing at first can get you thrown out at second on a hit. Watch the fielder: one running hard with their back to the infield probably won't catch it.
defense: Field it and throw to the lead base. An outfielder can get a force out at second if the runner waited at first.
common_mistakes: The runner waits at first on a ball over everyone's head and is forced out at second; the runner goes back to first while the batter also arrives, so two runners share one base; the runner goes halfway on a ball nobody could catch and only gets one base.

name: Dropped third strike, first base open
offense: Run! When the catcher doesn't catch strike three cleanly and first base is open, or there are two outs, the batter can run to first. Drop the bat and sprint until you're tagged, thrown out or called out. Don't wait for someone to tell you. This applies only where your league uses the uncaught-third-strike rule; many younger divisions don't.
defense: Catcher: pick the ball up and tag the batter or throw to first right away. First baseman: get to the base and give a target.
common_mistakes: The batter walks back toward the dugout; the batter waits for a coach to yell; the catcher rolls the ball back to the mound while the batter can still run.
